excerpts:
# Tailscale Funnel
## Get started with Funnel
### Requirements and limitations
Funnel requires the following to work:
* Tailscale v1.38.3 or later.
* [MagicDNS](/docs/features/magicdns) enabled for your tailnet.
* [HTTPS](/docs/how-to/set-up-https-certificates) enabled and valid HTTPS certificates for your tailnet.
* A funnel [node attribute](/docs/reference/syntax/policy-file#node-attributes) in your tailnet policy file.

...

* Funnel can only use DNS names in your [tailnet's domain](/docs/concepts/tailnet-name) (`tailnet-name.ts.net`).
* Funnel can only listen on ports `443`, `8443`, and `10000`.
* Funnel only works over [TLS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security)-encrypted connections.

...

## Troubleshooting
### Funnel node attribute
Tailscale Funnel requires a [node attribute](/docs/reference/syntax/policy-file#node-attributes) (`nodeAttrs`) of `funnel` in your tailnet policy file to tell Tailscale who can use Funnel. If you use the Tailscale CLI to enable Funnel, Tailscale ensures this requirement is met.

...

```json
"nodeAttrs": [
  {
    "target": ["autogroup:member"],
    "attr":   ["funnel"],
  },
],
```

...

### HTTPS certificates
Tailscale Funnel requires valid [HTTPS certificates](/docs/how-to/set-up-https-certificates) for your tailnet to automatically provision TLS certificates for your unique tailnet DNS name. If you use the Tailscale CLI to enable Funnel, Tailscale ensures this requirement is met.

# Tailscale Serve
> **Note:**The CLI commands for both [Tailscale Funnel](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/funnel) and [Tailscale Serve](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/serve) have changed in the 1.52 version of the Tailscale client. If you've used Funnel or Serve in previous versions, we recommend reviewing the CLI documentation.

...

## Get started with Serve
> **Warning:**Tailscale Serve requires you to enable HTTPS certificates in your tailnet.Additionally, keep in mind that [access control rules](/docs/features/access-control) apply to Serve just like any other service.

...

**Tailscale Funnel** is enabled by default. If you don't plan to use [Tailscale Funnel](/docs/features/tailscale-funnel) on the device, you can turn it off.

...

## Identity headers
You can use the identity headers with a custom backend or third-party services that offer authentication proxy authentication, such as [Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-security/configure-authentication/auth-proxy/#configure-auth-proxy-authentication).

...

## App capabilities header
> **Note:**Serve traffic can be configured to forward a header with selected app capabilities of the connected user or tagged device. Similar to identity headers, this isn't available for Funnel traffic, which is publicly available.This feature is available in Tailscale v1.92 or later.

...

## Limitations
* The same port number cannot be used for Serve (available only within the tailnet) and Funnel (available within the tailnet and to the public) at the same time.
* If the most recent command to configure the port was `serve`, then the port will be completely private.
* If the most recent command to configure the port was `funnel`, then the port will be completely public.

## Troubleshooting
Tailscale Serve requires that you [enable HTTPS](/docs/how-to/set-up-https-certificates) in your tailnet to automatically provision TLS certificates for your unique [tailnet DNS name](/docs/concepts/tailnet-name).

# Tailscale CLI
## Command Reference
### configure
* `--enable-startup=<init-system>` Install the startup script for the init system. The only currently supported value is `systemd`.
Examples:
* To configure your local `kubeconfig` file for authentication with a Kubernetes auth proxy:
```shell
tailscale configure kubeconfig <hostname-or-fqdn>
```

...

### funnel
Serve content and local servers from your Tailscale node to the internet.
To limit local service access to your tailnet, use the [`serve`](#serve) command.
```shell
tailscale funnel <target>
tailscale funnel <subcommand> [flags] <args>
```
Subcommands:
* [`status`](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/funnel#get-the-status) Gets the status.
* [`reset`](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/funnel#reset-tailscale-funnel) Resets the configuration.
For more information, refer to the [`tailscale funnel`](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/funnel) topic.

...

### serve
Serve content and local servers from your Tailscale node to your tailnet.
To publicly share the local service to the internet, use the [`funnel`](#funnel) command.
```shell
tailscale serve <target>
tailscale serve <subcommand> [flags] <args>
```

results.title: Tailscale Funnel examples
excerpts:
# Tailscale Funnel examples
Last validated Oct 14, 2025
> **Warning:**Before you try the examples in this topic, review the [Funnel documentation](/docs/features/tailscale-funnel) to make sure you meet the requirements.

...

## Share a simple file server
The following example uses the [`tailscale funnel`](/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/funnel) command to create a simple file server. Using Funnel as a file server is often more efficient than transferring through a third-party service. It's also more convenient than using tools like Python's `http.server`.

...

```shell
sudo tailscale funnel /tmp/public
```
On Windows, instead of using `sudo`, open the a command prompt as Administrator, then run:
```shell
c:\Users\Amelie> tailscale funnel c:\tmp\public
```
The status confirms the previous command and provides the hostname that Funnel configures for the device.

...

## Serve a static site
After you have your files, serve the static site to the internet:
```shell
sudo tailscale funnel /tmp/static-site
```
The status confirms the previous command and provides the hostname that Funnel configures for this device.

...

## Expose a development server to the public
If you have a local HTTP server running on port `3000`, you can expose the local server to the internet over HTTPS with Funnel:
```shell
sudo tailscale funnel 3000
```
The status confirms the previous command and provides the hostname that Funnel configures for this device.

...

## Share a Funnel device
You can share a Funnel device with a custom name. For example, a Funnel that exposes GitHub webhooks might have a name like `github-hooks-dev.pango-lin.ts.net`.
The follow command tuns on the Funnel for port `8080`:
```shell
sudo tailscale funnel 8080
```

1. Open the [DNS](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/dns) page of the admin console.
2. Enable [MagicDNS](/docs/features/magicdns#enabling-magicdns) if not already enabled for your tailnet.
3. Under **HTTPS Certificates**, select **Enable HTTPS**.
4.

...

### Machine names in the public ledger
[MagicDNS](/docs/features/magicdns) automatically registers DNS names for devices in your network, using their machine name. If the machine name changes, the MagicDNS
entry will change. You can [edit your machine name](/docs/concepts/machine-names#renaming-a-machine) to set it to a specific name.

...

If you obtain a TLS certificate for a node using MagicDNS, it will be accessible at both `https://machine-name.tailNNNN.ts.net`, using HTTPS, and also at `http://machine-name`, without HTTPS but using MagicDNS as a DNS nameserver.

## Encryption across Tailscale
Tailscale also uses encryption for authentication, secure node state storage , certificates , and features like the logging system and Tailnet Lock .

...

### Device TLS certificates
Tailscale assists you with provisioning TLS certificates from [Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/) using hostnames within your tailnet's MagicDNS domain . These certificates ensure only authorized devices in your tailnet can present valid service identities for MagicDNS hostnames.

# Host a website using a tailnet device
Alternatively, you can use the instructions below to host a website that is accessible to the public internet, using [Tailscale Funnel](/docs/features/tailscale-funnel).

## Prerequisites
* You need a [Tailscale account](/docs/how-to/quickstart).
* You need to [install Tailscale on your local machine](/download).
> **Note:**We recommend serving your files and website using a Linux VM. You can attempt this on macOS. However, due to the sandboxed nature of the operating system, you may encounter errors.
Here are instructions for creating various cloud-based Linux VMs and setting up Tailscale on your VM:
* [Create a Linux VM on Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/quick-create-portal?tabs=ubuntu)
* [Create a Linux VM on AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/EC2_GetStarted.html)
* [Create a Linux VM on GCP](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/create-linux-vm-instance)
After your Linux VM is created, you must also [install Tailscale on your Linux VM](/docs/install/linux).

...

## Serve your files and website
4. Run the following command on your machine to serve the `index.html` file to your tailnet:
  ```shell
  tailscale serve /tmp/test-funnel/index.html
  ```
Or, if you want to make the same files and website visible on the public internet, use the following command:

results.title: Tailscale Funnel: Share Your Web Server with the Public Internet
excerpts:
# Tailscale Funnel now available in beta
Branded artwork in greyscale
Tailscale Funnel, a tool that lets you share a web server on your private tailnet with the public internet, is now available as a beta feature for all users. With Funnel enabled, you can share access to a local development server, test a webhook, or even host a blog.
We got nerdsniped into simulating our logo going through a funnel.
Funnel provides a DNS name tied to your node that becomes publicly accessible once enabled. When a user on the public internet requests your service, we use a secure Tailscale tunnel to forward those requests along.
Given our commitment to user privacy, we’ve set up Funnel so we never see decrypted packets going to and from your service. All connections require TLS encryption, and Tailscale will automatically provision valid certificates with which your node does the TLS termination.
Because Funnel addresses are subdomains of ts.net, we could technically acquire valid certificates and do that termination server-side, but we believe that preserving user privacy is more important.
You can always confirm we haven’t obtained certificates for Funnel services by reviewing the public [Certificate Transparency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_Transparency) logs.

...

## What’s new since alpha
### DNS
Tailscale offers MagicDNS to resolve DNS requests for the names of nodes on your tailnet. This is a handy feature since remembering names ( `amelie.pango-lin.ts.net` ) is easier than remembering CGNAT IP addresses ( `100.x.y.z` ). Since launching Funnel alpha, we now need to forward `*.ts.net` DNS requests to a public resolver.

...

### CLI
```
 # You can now use any valid port for a `tailscale serve` command. # With the old CLI it was restricted to valid Funnel ports (443, 8443, 10000) ( OLD )  $ tailscale serve --serve-port = 222  tcp  22 # ERROR! ( NEW )  $ tailscale serve tcp:2222 tcp://localhost:22
```

## Now in beta
Tailscale Funnel is available in beta, which means you no longer need an invite to use it, but you will need to enable it in [your tailnet’s settings](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/settings/general) , and you’ll need to be running Tailscale 1.38.3 or later.
If you want to share how you’re using Funnel or other Tailscale features, we’d love to hear from you at devrel@tailscale.com !

# MagicDNS
If you add a new web server called `my-server` to your network, you no longer need to use its Tailscale IP: using the name `my-server` in your browser's address bar or on the command line will work.
![Example of a browser window with 'my-server' and a port number in the address bar.](features/magicdns/magic-dns.png)
> **Note:**MagicDNS does not require a [DNS nameserver](/docs/reference/dns-in-tailscale#tailscale-dns-settings) if running Tailscale v1.20 or later. Otherwise, your network must have **at least one DNS nameserver set** in the [DNS](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/dns) page of the admin console.

...

## Fully qualified domain names vs. machine names
The table below shows how some example machine names and domains combine to create the full domain name.
Machine Name
Tailnet Name
Fully Qualified Domain Name
monitoring
yak-bebop.ts.net
monitoring.yak-bebop.
ts.net
johns-iphone-6s
tailab12.ts.net
johns-iphone-6s.tailab12.
ts.net
free-form
example.ts.net
free-form.example.
ts.net

...

For the *yak-bebop* network, **the following two commands are equivalent**:
```shell
ping monitoring
ping monitoring.yak-bebop.ts.net
```
In most situations, you'll want to use the machine name. But for security reasons, accessing [devices shared with you](/docs/features/sharing) requires using the full domain name.
